content: Probiotics are live microorganisms that, when administered in sufficient quantities, may provide beneficial physiological effects. Some clinical trials have demonstrated that specific probiotic strains can help prevent respiratory infections. Although a prior review suggested that probiotics are beneficial for acute upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs), new studies have since been published, necessitating an updated review. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of probiotics, regardless of strain or dosage, compared to placebo or no treatment, in preventing acute URTIs across all age groups at risk for these infections. The search for relevant studies was extensive, covering multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and several Chinese literature databases, up to May 2022. Additionally, clinical trial registries were searched for completed and ongoing trials. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-RCTs that compared probiotics to placebo or no treatment for the prevention of acute URTIs. Participants included children, adults, and the elderly in various settings such as communities, schools, care facilities, and hospitals. Studies were excluded if they did not specifically address upper respiratory infections, involved more than 50% of participants vaccinated against influenza or other URTIs within the past year, or had significant differences in vaccination rates between study groups. Data collection and analysis were conducted independently by two reviewers using standard Cochrane methodologies. Both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses were performed, and a random-effects model was used for meta-analysis. Results were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included 23 individual RCTs and one cluster-RCT, involving a total of 6,950 participants. These participants ranged from children (aged 1 month to 11 years) to adults (mean age 37.3 years) and older adults (mean age 84.6 years). Probiotics were often administered with milk-based food in children, in powder form for adults, and either with milk-based food or in capsules for the elderly. Most studies used one or two probiotic strains, such as Lactobacillus plantarum HEAL9 or Lactobacillus paracasei (8700:2 or N1115), at doses of 10⁹ or 10¹¹ colony-forming units (CFU) per day for durations exceeding three months. The findings of the review were as follows: 1. Probiotics may reduce the number of participants diagnosed with at least one episode of URTIs (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.87; P < 0.001; 16 studies, 4,798 participants; low-certainty evidence). 2. Probiotics likely reduce the number of participants diagnosed with at least three episodes of URTIs (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.91; P = 0.02; 4 studies, 763 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). 3. Probiotics may reduce the incidence rate of URTIs (cases per person-year) (rate ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.92; P = 0.001; 12 studies, 4,364 participants; low-certainty evidence). 4. Probiotics may reduce the mean duration of an episode of acute URTIs by approximately 1.22 days (MD −1.22 days, 95% CI −2.12 to −0.33; P = 0.007; 6 studies, 2,406 participants; low-certainty evidence). 5. Probiotics likely reduce the number of participants who required prescribed antibiotics for acute URTIs (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.81; P = 0.001; 6 studies, 1,548 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). 6. Probiotics may not increase the number of participants experiencing at least one adverse event (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.15; P = 0.79; 8 studies, 2,456 participants; low-certainty evidence). 7. Evidence regarding the reduction in absenteeism from childcare, school, or work due to acute URTIs with probiotics is very uncertain (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.59; 1 study, 80 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Adverse events associated with probiotics were generally minor and most commonly involved gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting, flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that probiotics are more effective than placebo or no treatment in preventing acute URTIs. However, the certainty of evidence varies across outcomes, and further high-quality research is needed to confirm these findings.
